item.title: Thoracic — Positional Release / Counterstrain
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Thoracic and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: thoracic extension/rotation, posture-related symptoms and linked neck/shoulder comparable signs.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Prone, side-lying or supported sitting according to technique.
Use pillows as needed so breathing remains unrestricted.
therapistPosition: Stand close to the target level and use body weight rather than excessive arm force.
stabilization: Control the trunk/rib cage to localize the intended region and prevent rolling.
contact: Use broad contact over the intended thoracic or paraspinal target and avoid direct aggressive pressure on painful ribs.
Locate a reproducible tender point with light palpation, then monitor it while positioning the region toward maximal comfort.
Do not maintain painful pressure on the tender point.
forceDirection: The treatment direction is indirect: shorten/unload the painful tissue until tenderness is substantially reduced, then hold without force.
dosage: Traditional teaching often uses about 90 seconds, individualized to comfort and response.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Thoracic: thoracic extension/rotation, posture-related symptoms and linked neck/shoulder comparable signs.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Check trauma, osteoporosis/fracture risk, inflammatory disease and unexplained chest symptoms.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Thoracic assessment → correct regional setup → Positional Release / Counterstrain → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Thoracic Paraspinal Tender Point — Positional Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce focal thoracic guarding before active extension/rotation.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone, side-lying or supported sitting. Adjust thoracic flexion/extension, rotation and side-bending until tenderness falls markedly.
subTechniques.contact: Light monitoring contact over the tender paraspinal point.
subTechniques.direction: Maintain the position of maximal comfort without adding stretch.
subTechniques.dosage: 60–90 seconds, then return slowly to neutral.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The correct position is the one that reduces tenderness—not the one that looks most dramatic.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Use caution with osteoporosis and rib fracture risk.
